chunk_findings.detail: The two new pieces of documentation state opposite precedence for the diagnostics location. `DIAG_ENV`'s comment says the directory is "this variable, else `--diag-dir`, else `.ddflow/local/dryrun/`", i.e. the environment variable wins over the operator's explicit flag. The `Options.diag_dir` field comment says the field is what a failed run uses and "None: `DDFLOW_DRYRUN_DIAG_DIR`, else `<source>/.ddflow/local/dryrun`", i.e. when `--diag-dir` set the field, the flag wins and the env var is only consulted when the flag is absent. Concrete input: `DDFLOW_DRYRUN_DIAG_DIR=/var/log/ddflow` is exported and the operator runs with `--diag-dir /tmp/run7`; under the `DIAG_ENV` contract the transcript lands in `/var/log/ddflow` (possibly a shared, unwritable, or world-readable directory) even though an explicit directory was requested, while under the `Options` contract it lands in `/tmp/run7`. Whichever the code implements, the other statement is wrong about where a failed dry run's step table and stdout/stderr are written, and the two cannot both be authoritative for the environment-variable/flag interaction the intent calls out.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:DIAG_ENV vs Options.diag_dir

chunk_findings.detail: `MAX_COMMANDS = 300` is documented as "The most commands a transcript keeps (the last ones)", but the failure report added to `Result.render` prints `diagnostics (every step's stdout and stderr): <path>`, and the module bullet added in the same change promises the file holds "every command's bounded stdout and stderr". For a long rehearsal — a full upgrade dry run can easily emit more than 300 commands — the earlier commands' output is silently dropped from the file, so the artifact the operator is pointed at is missing exactly the earliest steps, while the report claims it is complete. Demonstrable: run a rehearsal that logs 400 commands and force it to fail; the JSON contains only the last 300 commands' streams, but the rendered table asserts "every step's stdout and stderr" are in it. The cap and the message need to agree (either raise/remove the cap or say the transcript is truncated to the last `MAX_COMMANDS` commands).

chunk_findings.detail: `live_moved` reports the union of `before.unstable` and `after.unstable`, i.e. shards that were already being written when the *pre-run* snapshot was read are surfaced as "the live shard {n} was still being written when read" and therefore make the run unavailable. That is a condition that existed before the rehearsal touched anything, so a live writer that was mid-append at snapshot time (and stops immediately after) is reported as a defect of the run. This is only masked by the whole-run retry; a writer that keeps churning makes every attempt fail. Arguably intended ("never as pass"), which is why this is only LOW.

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `shard_bytes_checked` (which returns both the shard bytes and the list of shards that "never held still") but keeps the pre-existing `shard_bytes` as `return shard_bytes_checked(repo)[0]`, i.e. it deliberately throws the `unstable` list away while keeping the same public name and signature. Under the scenario this change targets — a live writer appending to/rewriting a shard while step 10 snapshots it — `read_stable` returns `(torn_data, False)`, `shard_bytes_checked` stores that torn `data` in `out` *before* checking `stable`, and `shard_bytes` hands the dict to the caller with no way to tell it is a torn read. Any call site that still snapshots the live shards through `shard_bytes` therefore cannot produce the promised named result `'live repo changed during rehearsal'`: instead the torn before-snapshot flows into `prefixes_kept(before, after)`, which can report a phantom prefix loss (the same "unexplained dry-run failure under concurrent live writers," bug B-dryrun-flake), or, if the same torn bytes happen to land in both snapshots, a pass. The intent explicitly requires the rewrite to be reported as unavailable and "never as pass"; a lossy public wrapper that discards the only instability signal preserves exactly that hole. Either `shard_bytes` should be removed/guarded so all live-shard reads go through `shard_bytes_checked`, or it must not silently return bytes for shards whose `stable` flag is false.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py: `shard_bytes`

chunk_findings.detail: `add`'s second positional is the step's *display name* and the third is the *status* — see the two neighbouring calls in the same method, which pass the fixed name `"live project untouched"` with `False` (leaks) and `True` (clean). In the `moved` branch the author instead passes the outcome constant `LIVE_CHANGED` in the name slot and `None` in the status slot. Given input where a concurrent live writer rewrites a live shard (so `live_leaks(...)` is empty and `live_moved(...)` is non-empty), step 10 is recorded as a step *named* "live repo changed during rehearsal" with a null status. The named unavailable result the change promises ("reports a rewrite of a live shard as the named unavailable result … never as pass") therefore never lands in the status field: any consumer that keys on the status — the report renderer mapping a falsy status to FAIL, or the whole-run-retry check looking for the `LIVE_CHANGED` status — sees `None`/FAIL rather than the unavailable result, so a shard rewritten by another agent is reported as an ordinary failure. That is exactly the "upgrade-dry-run fails unexplained under concurrent live writers" symptom this change is meant to remove. The intended call is `self.add(10, name, LIVE_CHANGED, detail)` (name stays `"live project untouched"`, status carries the named unavailable result).

chunk_findings.detail: `footprint()` claims to return "what the rehearsal's own backups and snapshot tags (in the clones) are called", but it derives that identity purely as a set of *version* strings: it strips `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX` from each tag and runs `backup_versions(...)` over it, then hands `frozenset(versions)` to `Footprint`. Nothing in that set carries the run id the intent says attribution is keyed on, so `live_leaks(before, after, mine)` can only decide "this live tag/backup is the rehearsal's" by version. The motivating scenario makes this wrong: two concurrent dry runs of the same source produce the same tag/backup version (identical `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX<version>` names, since the name has no run id in it), so a tag or backup created in the live project by the *other* run lands in `mine`, is reported as this rehearsal's leak, and step 10 fails — the same unexplained failure under concurrent writers that this change exists to remove. The same over-attribution happens without any second run: `git clone --local` copies the live repo's refs/tags into `self.pristine`, so every `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX*` tag that already existed in the live repo at clone time is in the clone and therefore in `mine`, although the rehearsal never created it; a corresponding live tag is then attributable to this run. Conversely `judge_live`'s `others = set(after.tags) - set(before.tags)` (line ~806) uses a bare set difference with no run-id check either, so a genuine rehearsal leak whose version is not in `mine` is silently relabelled "made by others meanwhile and ignored" and the run passes. Either remove the tag scan (clone tags are the live repo's, not the rehearsal's) or key the footprint on the run id that the intent promises.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py `footprint` (called from `judge_live`)

chunk_findings.detail: Step 10 still hands the *pre-run* snapshot to `live_moved` and then treats any non-empty result as "the project moved under the run". `before` is the live read taken before the rehearsal started, so a shard that a live writer happened to be mid-append on at that instant (writer stops immediately afterwards, never touches the repo again while the dry run proceeds) is folded into `moved`, and step 10 is recorded as `LIVE_CHANGED` with the detail "...the project moved under the run, so it cannot be said to be untouched" — a condition that existed before the rehearsal touched anything. The earlier report of this is not answered by the new code: the new branch reports it as `unavailable` instead of `False`, but it still blames the run, still trips the whole-run retry, and on a repo with a slow writer it reproduces exactly the flake this change is meant to remove. The check should either ignore shards that were already unstable in `before`, or require the shard to have been readable/stable at the pre-run read before counting it as having moved.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's contract is that traces are attributed to the rehearsal "by run id", and tags do exactly that via `tag_owners`/`mine.tagger`; backups do not. `live_leaks` accepts a new backup as the rehearsal's whenever it is new, its stamp falls in `mine.started..mine.ended`, and its `<from>-to-<to>` is in `mine.versions`. In the multi-agent setting this change is written for, a concurrent agent running the *same* upgrade on the live repo produces exactly that: e.g. another agent upgrading 1.0→2.0 at 12:05:00 writes `.ddflow/backups/20261009T120500-1.0-to-2.0`, and with `mine = Footprint(started="...11:59:00", ended="...12:10:00", versions={"1.0-to-2.0"})` the guard `mine.started <= "20261009T120500" <= mine.ended` and `backup_versions(...) == "1.0-to-2.0"` both hold, so `live_leaks` returns "a backup of the rehearsal appeared in the live project: 20261009T120500-1.0-to-2.0" for a backup the rehearsal never made. The dry run then fails with a leak report — the same class of unexplained concurrent-writer flakiness (B-dryrun-flake) the change is meant to remove. Only an identifier actually carried by the artifact (as the tagger name is for tags) can distinguish the rehearsal's backup from another agent's; window+versions alone cannot.

chunk_findings.detail: Both the window test and the version extraction parse the backup name by splitting on the *first* hyphen, which is only valid if the `<stamp>` is hyphen-free, and the window test additionally requires `mine.started`/`mine.ended` to be in the identical string format as the stamp so that a lexicographic comparison means anything. If backups are stamped with an ISO-8601 time (e.g. `2026-10-09T12:05:00-1.0-to-2.0`), `b.partition("-")[0]` is `"2026"` (so the range check is vacuous/degenerate) and `backup_versions(b)` returns `"09T12:05:00-1.0-to-2.0"`, which never equals the `"1.0-to-2.0"` stored in `mine.versions`; likewise if `started`/`ended` are ISO while stamping is compact (or vice versa), the range comparison is decided by the first differing character ( `-` 0x2D vs `1` 0x31 ) and silently comes out false. In either case a *real* leaked rehearsal backup is never reported, i.e. the dry run passes/returns no problem despite the leak, contradicting "never as pass". A shared stamp formatter (or a parse to a comparable type) is needed instead of raw string comparison of two independently produced strings.

chunk_findings.detail: `half = limit // 2` is 0 for any `limit < 2`, and `text[-half:]` is then `text[-0:]`, i.e. `text[0:]` — the *entire* string. So `bounded("abcdef", limit=1)` returns `"\n... [6 characters cut] ...\nabcdef"`: it keeps every character while its own marker claims all 6 were cut, and the result is *longer* than the input. The function is exposed with a `limit` parameter, so any caller that passes a small bound (the only reason the parameter exists) silently gets an unbounded stream instead of a bounded one. The `half` value has to be clamped to at least 1 (or the `len(text) <= limit` branch widened) for the tail slice to be meaningful.

chunk_findings.detail: The diagnostics are gated on `any(c.status == FAIL ...) or report.facts.get("live_changed")` evaluated on the *final* report, but the retry path records a first-run movement under a different key (`report.facts["first_run"]`) and then throws the first run's report away. Concrete scenario: a concurrent writer touches a live shard once, so the first `_rehearse` sets `facts["live_changed"]` and the whole run is retried; the retry runs against a quiescent repo, all its checks pass, and `facts["live_changed"]` is absent on the second report. Now `report.facts["first_run"]` is set (the project demonstrably moved — the code sets it precisely to record this), `runs` contains two rehearsals and `write_diagnostics` would concatenate both runs' commands, yet the condition is false, so `write_diagnostics` is never called and `report.diagnostics` stays empty. That contradicts run_all's own docstring ("A failed run (or a project that moved) leaves its step table and every command's output in a file, named in the report") and discards exactly the captured command output needed to understand why the live shard looked rewritten. The condition needs to include `report.facts.get("first_run")` (set only in the retry branch) so a rehearsal that was restarted because the live repo moved still persists its evidence.

chunk_findings.detail: `footprint()` claims to return "what the rehearsal's own backups and snapshot tags (in the clones) are called", but it derives that identity purely as a set of *version* strings: it strips `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX` from each tag and runs `backup_versions(...)` over it, then hands `frozenset(versions)` to `Footprint`. Nothing in that set carries the run id the intent says attribution is keyed on, so `live_leaks(before, after, mine)` can only decide "this live tag/backup is the rehearsal's" by version. The motivating scenario makes this wrong: two concurrent dry runs of the same source produce the same tag/backup version (identical `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX<version>` names, since the name has no run id in it), so a tag or backup created in the live project by the *other* run lands in `mine`, is reported as this rehearsal's leak, and step 10 fails — the same unexplained failure under concurrent writers that this change exists to remove. The same over-attribution happens without any second run: `git clone --local` copies the live repo's refs/tags into `self.pristine`, so every `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX*` tag that already existed in the live repo at clone time is in the clone and therefore in `mine`, although the rehearsal never created it; a corresponding live tag is then attributable to this run. Conversely `judge_live`'s `others = set(after.tags) - set(before.tags)` (line ~806) uses a bare set difference with no run-id check either, so a genuine rehearsal leak whose version is not in `mine` is silently relabelled "made by others meanwhile and ignored" and the run passes. Either remove the tag scan (clone tags are the live repo's, not the rehearsal's) or key the footprint on the run id that the intent promises.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's contract is that traces are attributed to the rehearsal "by run id", and tags do exactly that via `tag_owners`/`mine.tagger`; backups do not. `live_leaks` accepts a new backup as the rehearsal's whenever it is new, its stamp falls in `mine.started..mine.ended`, and its `<from>-to-<to>` is in `mine.versions`. In the multi-agent setting this change is written for, a concurrent agent running the *same* upgrade on the live repo produces exactly that: e.g. another agent upgrading 1.0→2.0 at 12:05:00 writes `.ddflow/backups/20261009T120500-1.0-to-2.0`, and with `mine = Footprint(started="...11:59:00", ended="...12:10:00", versions={"1.0-to-2.0"})` the guard `mine.started <= "20261009T120500" <= mine.ended` and `backup_versions(...) == "1.0-to-2.0"` both hold, so `live_leaks` returns "a backup of the rehearsal appeared in the live project: 20261009T120500-1.0-to-2.0" for a backup the rehearsal never made. The dry run then fails with a leak report — the same class of unexplained concurrent-writer flakiness (B-dryrun-flake) the change is meant to remove. Only an identifier actually carried by the artifact (as the tagger name is for tags) can distinguish the rehearsal's backup from another agent's; window+versions alone cannot.

chunk_findings.detail: Both the window test and the version extraction parse the backup name by splitting on the *first* hyphen, which is only valid if the `<stamp>` is hyphen-free, and the window test additionally requires `mine.started`/`mine.ended` to be in the identical string format as the stamp so that a lexicographic comparison means anything. If backups are stamped with an ISO-8601 time (e.g. `2026-10-09T12:05:00-1.0-to-2.0`), `b.partition("-")[0]` is `"2026"` (so the range check is vacuous/degenerate) and `backup_versions(b)` returns `"09T12:05:00-1.0-to-2.0"`, which never equals the `"1.0-to-2.0"` stored in `mine.versions`; likewise if `started`/`ended` are ISO while stamping is compact (or vice versa), the range comparison is decided by the first differing character ( `-` 0x2D vs `1` 0x31 ) and silently comes out false. In either case a *real* leaked rehearsal backup is never reported, i.e. the dry run passes/returns no problem despite the leak, contradicting "never as pass". A shared stamp formatter (or a parse to a comparable type) is needed instead of raw string comparison of two independently produced strings.

chunk_findings.detail: `half = limit // 2` is 0 for any `limit < 2`, and `text[-half:]` is then `text[-0:]`, i.e. `text[0:]` — the *entire* string. So `bounded("abcdef", limit=1)` returns `"\n... [6 characters cut] ...\nabcdef"`: it keeps every character while its own marker claims all 6 were cut, and the result is *longer* than the input. The function is exposed with a `limit` parameter, so any caller that passes a small bound (the only reason the parameter exists) silently gets an unbounded stream instead of a bounded one. The `half` value has to be clamped to at least 1 (or the `len(text) <= limit` branch widened) for the tail slice to be meaningful.

chunk_findings.detail: The diagnostics are gated on `any(c.status == FAIL ...) or report.facts.get("live_changed")` evaluated on the *final* report, but the retry path records a first-run movement under a different key (`report.facts["first_run"]`) and then throws the first run's report away. Concrete scenario: a concurrent writer touches a live shard once, so the first `_rehearse` sets `facts["live_changed"]` and the whole run is retried; the retry runs against a quiescent repo, all its checks pass, and `facts["live_changed"]` is absent on the second report. Now `report.facts["first_run"]` is set (the project demonstrably moved — the code sets it precisely to record this), `runs` contains two rehearsals and `write_diagnostics` would concatenate both runs' commands, yet the condition is false, so `write_diagnostics` is never called and `report.diagnostics` stays empty. That contradicts run_all's own docstring ("A failed run (or a project that moved) leaves its step table and every command's output in a file, named in the report") and discards exactly the captured command output needed to understand why the live shard looked rewritten. The condition needs to include `report.facts.get("first_run")` (set only in the retry branch) so a rehearsal that was restarted because the live repo moved still persists its evidence.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff moves the "backup appeared during the run, for the versions it upgraded" check out of `live_leaks` and into `live_moved` (gated on `mine is not None`). The match condition is byte-for-byte the same (`mine.started <= b.partition("-")[0] <= mine.ended and backup_versions(b) in mine.versions`), so the *detection* is unchanged but the *classification* is downgraded from a certain leak to the ambiguous "moved" bucket. Concrete input: the live project has no such backup before step 10; during the run a backup named `<ts>-<version>` appears with `ts` inside `[mine.started, mine.ended]` and a version in `mine.versions` (i.e. exactly the signature of a rehearsal that wrote into the live repo). Before this change, `live_leaks` returned `"a backup of the rehearsal appeared in the live project: <b>"`, and step 10's `if leaks:` branch would `self.add(10, name, False, ...)` and return — an unambiguous failure. chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated contract is that `bounded` "keeps the ends", but none of the three assertions observes the tail. `bounded("abc", 10) == "abc"` only exercises the untruncated path; `len(bounded("x" * 1000, 100)) < 200` is homogeneous and only bounds the result loosely (a limit of 100 may legally produce up to 199 characters); `bounded("abcdef", 1) == "a"` pins the *head* for the degenerate case. A plain head-only implementation `s[:limit]` (or `s[:limit] + "…"`) satisfies every assertion, so the tail — precisely where a failing command's error text lives, which is why diagnostics need "bounded stdout/stderr" — can be silently dropped and this regression test still goes green. To actually test the promise you need a short input with distinct characters, e.g. `bounded("abcdefghij", 6)` must both start with the original prefix and end with the original suffix; no assertion of that form exists.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's contract is that traces are attributed to the rehearsal "by run id", and tags do exactly that via `tag_owners`/`mine.tagger`; backups do not. `live_leaks` accepts a new backup as the rehearsal's whenever it is new, its stamp falls in `mine.started..mine.ended`, and its `<from>-to-<to>` is in `mine.versions`. In the multi-agent setting this change is written for, a concurrent agent running the *same* upgrade on the live repo produces exactly that: e.g. another agent upgrading 1.0→2.0 at 12:05:00 writes `.ddflow/backups/20261009T120500-1.0-to-2.0`, and with `mine = Footprint(started="...11:59:00", ended="...12:10:00", versions={"1.0-to-2.0"})` the guard `mine.started <= "20261009T120500" <= mine.ended` and `backup_versions(...) == "1.0-to-2.0"` both hold, so `live_leaks` returns "a backup of the rehearsal appeared in the live project: 20261009T120500-1.0-to-2.0" for a backup the rehearsal never made. The dry run then fails with a leak report — the same class of unexplained concurrent-writer flakiness (B-dryrun-flake) the change is meant to remove. Only an identifier actually carried by the artifact (as the tagger name is for tags) can distinguish the rehearsal's backup from another agent's; window+versions alone cannot.

chunk_findings.detail: Both the window test and the version extraction parse the backup name by splitting on the *first* hyphen, which is only valid if the `<stamp>` is hyphen-free, and the window test additionally requires `mine.started`/`mine.ended` to be in the identical string format as the stamp so that a lexicographic comparison means anything. If backups are stamped with an ISO-8601 time (e.g. `2026-10-09T12:05:00-1.0-to-2.0`), `b.partition("-")[0]` is `"2026"` (so the range check is vacuous/degenerate) and `backup_versions(b)` returns `"09T12:05:00-1.0-to-2.0"`, which never equals the `"1.0-to-2.0"` stored in `mine.versions`; likewise if `started`/`ended` are ISO while stamping is compact (or vice versa), the range comparison is decided by the first differing character ( `-` 0x2D vs `1` 0x31 ) and silently comes out false. In either case a *real* leaked rehearsal backup is never reported, i.e. the dry run passes/returns no problem despite the leak, contradicting "never as pass". A shared stamp formatter (or a parse to a comparable type) is needed instead of raw string comparison of two independently produced strings.

chunk_findings.detail: `half = limit // 2` is 0 for any `limit < 2`, and `text[-half:]` is then `text[-0:]`, i.e. `text[0:]` — the *entire* string. So `bounded("abcdef", limit=1)` returns `"\n... [6 characters cut] ...\nabcdef"`: it keeps every character while its own marker claims all 6 were cut, and the result is *longer* than the input. The function is exposed with a `limit` parameter, so any caller that passes a small bound (the only reason the parameter exists) silently gets an unbounded stream instead of a bounded one. The `half` value has to be clamped to at least 1 (or the `len(text) <= limit` branch widened) for the tail slice to be meaningful.

chunk_findings.detail: The diagnostics are gated on `any(c.status == FAIL ...) or report.facts.get("live_changed")` evaluated on the *final* report, but the retry path records a first-run movement under a different key (`report.facts["first_run"]`) and then throws the first run's report away. Concrete scenario: a concurrent writer touches a live shard once, so the first `_rehearse` sets `facts["live_changed"]` and the whole run is retried; the retry runs against a quiescent repo, all its checks pass, and `facts["live_changed"]` is absent on the second report. Now `report.facts["first_run"]` is set (the project demonstrably moved — the code sets it precisely to record this), `runs` contains two rehearsals and `write_diagnostics` would concatenate both runs' commands, yet the condition is false, so `write_diagnostics` is never called and `report.diagnostics` stays empty. That contradicts run_all's own docstring ("A failed run (or a project that moved) leaves its step table and every command's output in a file, named in the report") and discards exactly the captured command output needed to understand why the live shard looked rewritten. The condition needs to include `report.facts.get("first_run")` (set only in the retry branch) so a rehearsal that was restarted because the live repo moved still persists its evidence.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff moves the "backup appeared during the run, for the versions it upgraded" check out of `live_leaks` and into `live_moved` (gated on `mine is not None`). The match condition is byte-for-byte the same (`mine.started <= b.partition("-")[0] <= mine.ended and backup_versions(b) in mine.versions`), so the *detection* is unchanged but the *classification* is downgraded from a certain leak to the ambiguous "moved" bucket. Concrete input: the live project has no such backup before step 10; during the run a backup named `<ts>-<version>` appears with `ts` inside `[mine.started, mine.ended]` and a version in `mine.versions` (i.e. exactly the signature of a rehearsal that wrote into the live repo). Before this change, `live_leaks` returned `"a backup of the rehearsal appeared in the live project: <b>"`, and step 10's `if leaks:` branch would `self.add(10, name, False, ...)` and return — an unambiguous failure. After this change, `live_leaks` returns nothing for it and `live_moved(before, after, mine)` returns `"a backup appeared in the live project while the rehearsal ran, for its versions (another agent's upgrade, or a leak): <b>"`, which step 10 routes to the named `LIVE_CHANGED` ("live repo changed during rehearsal") result with one whole-run retry. Because the retry re-baselines (`before` on the retry already contains the backup the first attempt leaked), the delta `set(after.backups) - set(before.backups)` is empty on the second pass, so the leaked backup is not reported at all and the run can finish as a pass. chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated contract is that `bounded` "keeps the ends", but none of the three assertions observes the tail. `bounded("abc", 10) == "abc"` only exercises the untruncated path; `len(bounded("x" * 1000, 100)) < 200` is homogeneous and only bounds the result loosely (a limit of 100 may legally produce up to 199 characters); `bounded("abcdef", 1) == "a"` pins the *head* for the degenerate case. A plain head-only implementation `s[:limit]` (or `s[:limit] + "…"`) satisfies every assertion, so the tail — precisely where a failing command's error text lives, which is why diagnostics need "bounded stdout/stderr" — can be silently dropped and this regression test still goes green. To actually test the promise you need a short input with distinct characters, e.g. `bounded("abcdefghij", 6)` must both start with the original prefix and end with the original suffix; no assertion of that form exists.

chunk_findings.detail: `maybe_leaked` ignores its run counter (`_n`) and unconditionally does `(root / ".ddflow" / "backups" / f"{stamp}-0.2.1-to-0.9").mkdir(parents=True)` where `stamp = DR.clock.compact_at()`. The change also (correctly) asserts `len(calls) == 2`, i.e. the hook now runs twice in the same live `root` (the whole-run retry). If `compact_at()` yields the same value on the second run — which happens whenever the dry-run clock is frozen for reproducibility, or simply because both runs land in the same clock tick, since the retry is immediate — then the second invocation calls `mkdir` on a path already created by the first invocation and raises `FileExistsError` instead of performing the leak. Either the test errors out or the second run's detection is no longer exercising what the assertion claims; the analogous first test was adjusted for the retry (`rewrite_once` now issues a `git` command) but this hook was not made idempotent (`exist_ok=True`, or guarding on `_n == 1`).
